# Page 3^page=3
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 1 Executive Summary The Aquatic Invasive Species Summit, hosted on March 27, 2026 by Saskatchewan Ministry of Trade and Export Development and the Pacific Northwest Economic Region (PNWER), convened about 50 state, provincial, and federal leaders from across the region to assess current mussel prevention and inspection efforts, review lessons learned from infested jurisdictions, and identify opportunities to strengthen regional coordination. Discussions reinforced that aquatic invasive mussels pose a substantial threat to regional hydropower, irrigation, municipal water systems, trade infrastructure, cultural sites, and aquatic ecosystems. While the PNWER region remains largely uninfested, speakers emphasized that the opportunity to prevent widespread infestation is narrowing and will require sustained commitment and collaboration on prevention efforts. A central theme throughout the summit was the region’s continued success at preventing established infestation of mussels. This has been accomplished through collaboration on sharing data, tools, and operational experience to prevent infestation. The region remaining largely mussel free is due to strong coordination and implementation of inspection stations across the region. Summit speakers emphasized the need to continue investing in inspection and decontamination capacity, improve regional standardization of protocols, strengthen data sharing and vessel tracking, enhance border and corridor interception efforts, and maintain long-term support for rapid response readiness. Presentations highlighted that watercraft inspection and decontamination programs remain the most practical and cost-effective line of defense against invasive mussel introduction. Jurisdictions across the region have made significant progress in building inspection capacity, sharing data, expanding use of tools such as K9 detection teams, and increasing Canada-U.S. border inspection efforts. At the same time, presenters noted that different standards, fragmented data systems, and varying enforcement authorities across jurisdictions continue to create vulnerabilities within the broader prevention framework. Experiences shared by Manitoba and Idaho demonstrated the substantial financial and operational requirements that follow a detection or established infestation, reinforcing that prevention remains significantly less costly than containment and mitigation. The summit showcased that while meaningful progress has been made, the next phase of advancement will require jurisdictions to move beyond informal collaboration toward a more integrated regional prevention system capable of operating consistently and effectively across borders.

# Page 4^page=4
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 2 Purpose The AIS Summit was proposed and designed to strengthen Saskatchewan and the region’s preparedness and coordination capacity related to watercraft inspection for quagga and zebra mussel aquatic invasive species (AIS) detection. Prevention remains the most cost-effective strategy for PNWER jurisdictions. If mussels were to be established in the region, the costs associated for containment and treatment of an AIS infestation would be substantial. The summit was an opportunity to showcase experiences from jurisdictions demonstrating that successful prevention depends on having plans, watercraft inspection programs, and coordinated stakeholder engagement plans in place before an incident occurs. The summit provided a forum to bring together partners and other critical stakeholders to improve understanding of Saskatchewan’s current plans and identify opportunities to strengthen readiness. Through collaborative dialogue and shared learning, participants highlighted best practices, lessons learned from other jurisdictions, and the operational, regulatory, and funding considerations necessary to support an effective watercraft inspection program and response once a detection occurs. The summit was designed to convene key decision-makers and operational staff to educate them about the issue and develop recommendations from the presentations and panel discussions. # Page 5^page=5
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 3 Session Summaries Introductions and Welcome – Opening Remarks • MLA Travis Keisig | Last Mountain-Touchwood and PNWER President • Honourable Darlene Rowden | Saskatchewan Ministry of Environment MLA Travis Keisig kicked off the summit with an overview of the challenges that aquatic invasive species (AIS) – specifically quagga, zebra, and golden mussels – pose to the region. He noted that the goal of the summit was to showcase the current work being undertaken and what the region can do to preserve and protect our waterways and ecosystems. The Honourable Darlene Rowden, Saskatchewan Minister of Environment, provided remarks about the direct threat AIS brings to the Saskatchewan and regional economy, highlighting hydropower, agriculture, irrigation, municipal water, and trade corridors as sectors and infrastructure that could be impacted. The Minister made it clear that jurisdictions should continue the great work to prevent the introduction of invasive mussels to the region that will create costly ongoing mitigation and public investment. She emphasized the importance of continued collaboration to address invasive species risks. Watercraft Inspection Across the PNWER Region • Martina Beck | British Columbia Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship, PNWER Invasive Species Co-Chair Martina Beck provided insights on current mussel prevention efforts underway across the region. She discussed ongoing challenges and emphasized watercraft inspection programs as the most practical and immediate line of defense. Jurisdictions have made meaningful progress in sharing data and coordinating detection and response efforts across borders. At the same time, each jurisdiction operates under its own standards, authorities, and programmatic approaches. As boats move between jurisdictions, differing requirements, inspection processes, and enforcement practices can create gaps in the broader prevention framework. Individual programs are performing well within their respective systems, but greater alignment would strengthen the region’s collective ability to build a more seamless and comprehensive prevention network. The session explored how the work underway enhances regional readiness. Additionally, securing community and legislative support is important to sustaining successful prevention programs.

# Page 6^page=6
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 4 Balancing Prevention and Containment in a Mussel Invaded Landscape ● Jeff Long | Manitoba Department of Environment and Climate Change Jeff Long provided a sobering view of the current challenges in Manitoba. With existing zebra mussel establishment in one of Canada’s largest freshwater lakes, the containment efforts to prevent further spread within Manitoba and into the PNWER region are stretched to current capacity. Much of the work is to triage the problem and continue to share information on detections close to the Saskatchewan border. The presentation noted the reality of the situation by outlining what happens once invasive mussels establish. Prevention and containment are implemented based on the best information and resources available. Prevention is targeted, finite, and cost efficient. Containment is indefinite, resource intensive, and focused on limiting damage rather than avoiding it. Experiences from infested jurisdictions like Manitoba raise an important question for PNWER jurisdictions: do we pivot the communication of “preventing” mussel infestation to “delaying” infestation? The long-term financial burden associated with invasive mussel infestation is significant and ongoing. Idaho’s recent containment and treatment response shows the cost and resources needed to address a detection. The session underscored that robust prevention efforts can delay or avoid infestation altogether, reducing future containment and mitigation costs. In practical terms, underinvesting in prevention today increases the likelihood of far greater long term financial obligations tomorrow. Snake River Response Update ● Lloyd Knight | Idaho State Department of Agriculture The Snake River case study spotlighted Idaho’s response to an invasive mussel detection. In September 2023, quagga mussels were first detected near Twin Falls, Idaho in the Snake River, a large tributary of the Columbia River. They were again detected in the same area in 2024 and 2025. The two response efforts were a complex, resource intensive, and time sensitive event that required coordination among numerous state, federal, and local agencies. Decisions had to be made quickly, often with incomplete information, while multiple agencies worked in parallel. It was noted several times that support from the Governor was critical to ensuring state agencies coordinated effectively and that funding was available to meet response needs. The case reinforced that response is not simply an extension of prevention programs. It requires its own structure, authority, and funding. Additionally, response must be tailored to the specific waterbody and circumstance of the mussel detection. As jurisdictions develop their response strategies, flexibility based on location and conditions will be essential. The case also raised an important question: if a detection occurred tomorrow, would jurisdictions know exactly how

# Page 7^page=7
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 5 treatment or response teams would cross state or provincial borders, what actions would need to be taken in advance, and how would those actions be funded? Biosecurity at the International Border • Brendan Spearin | Fisheries and Oceans Canada Brendan Spearin provided an overview of the border inspection operations in Manitoba. The international border represents one of the few locations where fouled watercraft and equipment can be intercepted in a controlled and predictable manner before entering Canada. The presentation highlighted that while border crossings offer a strategic opportunity for prevention, aquatic invasive species screening is not yet fully embedded into all standard border operations. AIS inspections are limited and compete with broader priorities tied to customs, security, and trade facilitation. Frontline personnel play a vital role in protecting regional waterways, and continued inspection and training will further strengthen the region’s ability to manage AIS risks. Building these capabilities presents a significant opportunity to improve border inspections. The discussion raised an important policy consideration: if border crossings are to function as a meaningful control point, AIS prevention must be elevated from a secondary consideration to a core operational responsibility. Additionally, implementing fees for arriving fouled watercraft is under consideration as a policy option to replace the current approach of issuing warnings without monetary penalties. Without stronger integration, coordination, and alignment across agencies and countries, the burden of interception shifts downstream to inland inspection stations and local response programs, where options become narrower and costs increase substantially. Third-Party Inspection Program: Benefits and Challenges ● Tom Woolf | Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks Third-party inspection programs are an important option to offset capacity constraints and are a necessary tool in building a more comprehensive inspection network. Contracted inspection providers can expand geographic coverage, extend operating hours, and help jurisdictions maintain inspection presence in high-traffic corridors or remote locations where staffing government-operated stations may be difficult. The session showcased that these programs introduce new risks if not properly managed. Variability in training, oversight, and accountability can create inconsistencies that undermine the broader system.

# Page 8^page=8
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 6 Without strong certification requirements, clear contractual expectations, and regular performance oversight, third-party providers risk introducing unintended gaps into the system. The broader policy question raised by the session is whether jurisdictions are treating third-party inspection as a strategic extension of their AIS program or merely as a staffing solution. The distinction will determine whether these programs enhance prevention capacity or dilute it. PANEL: Strengthening Regional Response to High-Risk Watercraft • Moderated by Jeri Geiger | Saskatchewan Ministry of Environment • Matt Tyree | Saskatchewan Ministry of Environment • Martina Beck | British Columbia Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship • Samantha Clinton | Alberta Environment and Protected Areas • Tom Woolf | Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks • Jeff Long | Manitoba Department of Environment and Climate Change The panel discussion highlighted the tremendous progress jurisdictions across the PNWER region have made in strengthening their aquatic invasive species prevention and response programs. Panelists demonstrated that states and provinces have developed increasingly sophisticated inspection, decontamination, and enforcement systems, with each jurisdiction adapting its program to local needs while building operational expertise. This overview showcased the growing regional commitment to preventing the spread of invasive mussels and other aquatic invasive species through proactive management of watercraft inspection. A major success identified throughout the discussion was the increased level of coordination and communication now occurring between jurisdictions when vessels are detected or pass through a jurisdiction. Agencies regularly share data, notifying neighboring jurisdictions of intercepted vessels, and working together to manage risks before they escalate. While systems continue to evolve, panelists emphasized that regional relationships and trust between program leads have improved in recent years, creating a stronger foundation for coordinated action than previously existed. Panelists also noted that jurisdictions are deploying more tools and working to increase enforcement and inspection. Programs are increasingly prioritizing areas of concern, known travel corridors, and repeat offenders to make better use of limited resources. This effort reflects a shift from general inspections and more targeted operations that improve efficiency and strengthen overall prevention outcomes.

# Page 9^page=9
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 7 Conversely, the discussion acknowledged that high-risk watercraft continue to present a uniquely regional challenge because vessel movement routinely crosses jurisdictional boundaries. A watercraft that bypasses or is inadequately inspected in one jurisdiction can quickly create downstream risk for neighboring states and provinces. This reality reinforces the importance of continued work toward stronger interoperability between programs, including improved information sharing, more consistent enforcement authorities, and clearer regional protocols for managing high-risk vessel movements. Overall, the panel demonstrated that the region has made meaningful progress in building a more coordinated and capable response network for high-risk watercraft. The success of current efforts reflects not only stronger individual programs but also a growing recognition that no single jurisdiction can manage the threat alone. The discussion made clear that the next phase of advancement will require moving beyond informal coordination toward more integrated regional systems that allow jurisdictions to operate with greater consistency and speed across borders. The foundation for that work is now in place, and the region is better positioned than ever to build upon it. Use of K9s for AIS Prevention ● Cindy Sawchuk | Alberta Environment and Protected Areas The presentation highlighted the growing success of K9 detection programs as a valuable enhancement to aquatic invasive species inspection efforts. Trained detection dogs have proven to be highly effective at identifying invasive mussels and residual water contamination quickly and accurately, allowing inspectors to process vessels more efficiently while improving detection capability. Their speed and sensitivity make them particularly useful during inspections where visual inspections alone may be insufficient or time consuming. K9 programs have also emerged as a strong public engagement tool. The visibility of detection dogs at inspection stations draws public attention, creates positive interactions with boaters, and helps reinforce awareness of AIS prevention requirements. This added outreach benefit can improve compliance and make inspection stops more approachable while still supporting enforcement objectives. The presentation demonstrated that K9 units can strengthen both the technical and public-facing sides of an AIS program when deployed effectively. The discussion emphasized that K9 teams are most effective when integrated into a broader inspection and enforcement framework. They are not a replacement for strong inspection programs, standardized protocols, or enforcement authority but rather a force multiplier within a well-structured system. The success seen in Alberta’s program suggests that jurisdictions willing to treat K9 detection as a strategic long-term investment, rather than a supplemental add-on, can significantly improve overall inspection capacity and prevention outcomes.

# Page 10^page=10
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 8 Closing Remarks ● MLA Travis Keisig | Last Mountain-Touchwood and President of PNWER The closing remarks reinforced a consistent message that carried through the entire summit: the region still has an opportunity to prevent widespread infestation, but that opportunity is diminishing. The tools, knowledge, and examples are already in place. The challenge is moving from discussion to implementation. The final takeaway is difficult but clear. The region is not facing a knowledge gap. It is facing a coordination and execution gap. If jurisdictions continue to operate independently with inconsistent systems, the outcome is predictable. If they move toward alignment, standardization, and sustained investment, there is still a path to avoiding long term consequences. Takeaways & Next Steps Across all sessions, a pattern emerged – the issue is not whether programs exist, it is whether they function together as a system. Inconsistent standards, fragmented data, and uneven enforcement create openings that invasive species will exploit. The summit points to a single conclusion. The region must decide whether it is willing to operate as a coordinated system or continue managing risk jurisdiction by jurisdiction. That decision will determine whether prevention remains viable or whether containment becomes the default reality. Next Steps 1. Sustain and Expand Inspection Capacity – Continue investing in robust watercraft inspection and decontamination programs as the primary line of defense against mussel introduction. PNWER will continue to advocate with partners to Canadian and U.S. federal governments about funding and promoting best practices about how to economically maximize available resources. 2. Continue Regional Coordination – Promoting and sharing best practices on inspection protocols, decontamination standards, enforcement approaches, and operational procedures across jurisdictions will reduce gaps and create a more seamless regional prevention network. 3. Strengthen Data Sharing and Risk-Based Operations – Where available, partners should share communication and vessel tracking between jurisdictions to improve situational awareness and support targeted inspection and enforcement efforts focused on high-risk watercraft, repeat offenders, and priority travel corridors.

# Page 11^page=11
Aquatic Invasive Species Summit Report | 9 4. Enhance Border and Interception Capabilities – Explore how other border crossings can learn from Manitoba and increase AIS prevention efforts at key entry points along the Canada-U.S. border. 5. Maintain Long-Term Program Funding – PNWER will collaborate with legislators to continue sustained support for prevention programs while continuing to encourage federal investment through annual budget processes. 6. Sustained AIS Summit program – PNWER will explore options for member jurisdictions to host an AIS Summit on an annual basis. Rotating the summit across jurisdictions will support broad participation and shared collaboration throughout the region. These forums play a critical role in strengthening relationships, educating critical infrastructure owners and operators, and improving alignment across programs. The goal is to ensure jurisdictions understand each other’s policies and technologies as threats and risks from invasive mussels evolve.
